analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the 20% tax deduction for pass-through business income.
analysis.headline: The bill to make the pass-through tax deduction permanent never left the Senate Finance Committee and received no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 tax law created a deduction letting owners of pass-through businesses — partnerships, S-corporations, and LLCs — exclude 20% of their business income from federal tax, but set it to expire after 2025. This bill would strike that expiration and make the deduction permanent. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2019 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of pass-through businesses, which include most partnerships, S-corporations, LLCs, and sole proprietorships. While the deduction is available to ordinary small business owners, the largest dollar benefits flow to the highest-earning business owners, since the deduction is worth 20% of whatever qualified income a business reports. Making it permanent also removes the deadline that would otherwise force a future Congress to decide all over again whether to keep it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deletes the section of the tax code that sunsets the qualified business income deduction after December 31, 2025, making the deduction permanent.
The deduction lets owners of pass-through businesses exclude 20% of qualified business income from federal tax.
Its stated purpose, in the short title, is 'Main Street Tax Certainty' — giving small business owners confidence the deduction will not lapse.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally. Permanently extending a tax deduction means the revenue is never collected; the 2017 law's drafters used the expiration date partly to keep the bill's official cost down, and striking it locks in that cost indefinitely unless a future Congress raises taxes or cuts spending elsewhere.

drawbacks.text: Making the deduction permanent removes the 2025 expiration that currently limits its cost, converting a temporary tax cut into a permanent reduction in federal revenue that adds to deficits unless offset.

The deduction's benefits scale with business income, so the largest tax savings go to the owners of the most profitable pass-through businesses — including partnerships and LLCs whose owners are among the highest earners — rather than being targeted to small main-street firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real benefit for some genuinely small business owners, who gain certainty about a deduction they currently use. But the cost is one-sided: permanence means the largest deductions — which go to the highest-earning business owners — continue indefinitely, with no sunset forcing a future debate about whether the tax break is worth its revenue cost. The bill's 'Main Street' framing sits awkwardly beside a structure whose dollar benefits concentrate at the top of the income distribution.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Daines introduced the bill on April 11, 2019, joined by original cosponsors Senators Roberts and Thune.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The bill had four Republican cosponsors.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the bill's complete action history before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody gained the permanent tax cut. Owners of highly profitable pass-through businesses keep facing the deduction's scheduled 2025 expiration, and the federal Treasury avoids an open-ended revenue loss — though ordinary small business owners also keep facing the uncertainty the bill's sponsors cited.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; no tax cut happened

industries.industry: High-earning pass-through business owners (partnerships, S-corps, LLCs)
industries.note: The bill would lock in a 20% exclusion of business income from federal tax permanently, with the largest dollar benefits going to owners of the most profitable firms. The cost is permanent federal revenue that would otherwise fund public purposes or reduce deficits.

Genuinely small pass-through firms also use the deduction and would gain certainty that it does not lapse in 2025. Their share of the total benefit is smaller than the share going to the largest firms.

Rental and investment partnerships qualify for the deduction without the income limits that apply to certain professional services firms, so permanence is worth the most to large real estate and investment partnerships. Their gain comes at the Treasury's expense.
